text: The circuit you write in QuantumCircuit is an abstract plan — you call h, cx, ccx without worrying about what a physical chip can actually do. Transpilation is the real, necessary translation step that turns that abstract plan into something a specific backend can physically execute.

transpile with a target backend and an optimization level does two things at once: it rewrites every gate into the backend's native basis gate set, and it maps your circuit's logical qubits onto the backend's physical qubits, respecting the coupling map from the previous lesson. The result, compiled, is the circuit that actually gets sent to hardware — not qc itself.

Here's a real before-and-after from IBM's own Qiskit documentation. Before transpilation: a two-qubit circuit with a Hadamard gate and two CNOT gates, written the way you'd naturally write it in QuantumCircuit.

After transpilation, the same circuit uses RZ, X, SX, and ECR gates — the backend's actual native basis set. Nothing about what the circuit computes changed, but every gate you wrote has been rewritten into gates the hardware can physically execute.

Here's a well-documented fact you don't need to simulate to verify: a single Toffoli gate, decomposed into CX plus single-qubit gates, standardly expands into 6 CNOT gates plus several single-qubit H, T, and T-dagger gates. A circuit that looks compact with a handful of Toffoli gates in your source code can balloon into dozens of CNOTs once transpiled — and that's before routing adds any further overhead for a specific backend's connectivity.

Optimization level, 0 through 3, controls how hard the transpiler works to shrink the circuit, trading compile time for a smaller result — and on noisy real hardware, where every extra gate is another chance for error, higher levels usually matter more than they do in simulation. Routing inserts SWAP gates when a two-qubit gate's targets aren't physically adjacent, and each SWAP is itself built from multiple native two-qubit gates. The practical lesson: how many gates your circuit has is not answerable from qc alone — always check compiled.count_ops() and compiled.depth() on the transpiled circuit for your actual target backend.
Next lesson follows a transpiled circuit into the real world: what happens after you submit a job, how to check on it, and how to manage it without babysitting a running notebook.
